data.title: Klučov – one of the oldest Slavic hillforts in Bohemia
data.excerpt: Detailed excavation of this Slavic hillfort took place in the 1950s and showed that it held an important status as a seat of power. Founded in the middle of the 8th century, Klučov is one of the oldest fortified hilltop sites in Bohemia, Moravia and Slovakia, and it is notable for its tower gateway and for an underground passage leading down to the river.
data.metaTitle: Klučov – one of the oldest Slavic hillforts in Bohemia
data.metaDescription: A Slavic hillfort above the river Šembera, founded in the middle of the 8th century; excavation in the 1950s confirmed its status as a seat of power.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: A rise in the cadastral area of the village of Klučov, sloping southwards into the valley; the river Šembera flows through the area

keyFacts.label: Significance
keyFacts.value: One of the oldest hillforts of its type (a fortified hilltop site) in Bohemia, Moravia and Slovakia

keyFacts.label: Defensive network
keyFacts.value: Together with the hillforts of Přistoupim, Doubravčice and Tismice it formed a defensive and economic base beside an important trade route

keyFacts.label: The earlier (inner) defences
keyFacts.value: A timber-and-earth rampart with a ditch, in places a barrier of vertically and obliquely set posts — with no use of stone

keyFacts.label: The tower gateway
keyFacts.value: About 7 m wide, projecting in front of the rampart, the passage 11–12 m long, with a raised storey and loopholes

keyFacts.label: The secret passage
keyFacts.value: An underground passage at the north-western edge of the hillfort ran obliquely down to the level of the river — access to water during a siege

keyFacts.label: Height of the rampart
keyFacts.value: Approximately 2.5 m, reinforced by a ditch immediately in front of it

keyFacts.label: Internal buildings
keyFacts.value: Slavic semi-sunken buildings and a larger number of granaries — pits for storing grain and food

children.text: Detailed excavation of this Slavic hillfort took place in the 1950s, and it established that this was a hillfort with an important status as a seat of power.
The site and the Slavic occupation

The site of the hillfort lies today in the cadastral area of the village of Klučov. The rise on which the Slavic hillfort extended is today used for farming. The Slavic hillfort stood on a knoll that slopes southwards into the valley. The river Šembera, its branches and its tributaries flow through the area. This strategic position in hilly terrain was already used by the first Slavic tribes.

The founding of the hillfort itself, and at the same time of the inner defences, is dated to the middle of the 8th century, while its demise is then assumed a century later. Besides the Slavic occupation, however, Neolithic traces were also uncovered at the site. A ditch connected with the defences of a settlement of the Únětice culture dates from the Early Bronze Age. After the demise of the Slavic hillfort the knoll was still used for a short time as a Hussite military camp.

The archaeological importance of the hillfort site at Klučov lies precisely in the time of its founding. It is one of the oldest hillforts of its type (a fortified hilltop site) in Bohemia, Moravia and Slovakia. The hillfort lay in an area where, together with other hillforts (Přistoupim, Doubravčice and Tismice), it formed a defensive and economic base beside an important trade route. Various specialised crafts were traced inside the hillfort, while farming, on the other hand, was evidently pushed out beyond the line of the defences into the neighbouring hamlets.

The earlier defences of Klučov consisted of a timber-and-earth rampart with a ditch and, in places, a barrier of vertically and obliquely set posts. The later defences are then represented by a timber-and-earth rampart and a frontal gateway inserted into the gap in the interrupted ditch. No stone was used in the construction of the rampart. This stoneless construction is typical of the first Slavic hillforts. The earlier rampart of the defences is also described as the inner one, because the later rampart partly surrounded it.

The earlier phase of the defences occupied the whole area of the top of the knoll. The defences consisted of a timber-and-earth rampart with a ditch in front of it; in some stretches the remains of a further defensive element were recognised, a barrier set out in front of the ditch and formed of upright and oblique posts. The earlier phase of the defences ran out eastwards into a point, where access to the hillfort was built in the form of a side gateway.

The later phase of the defences consisted of a rampart built in the first half of the 9th century on the eastern side, which abutted with its southern and northern ends on the inner defences of the hillfort. In front of the rampart there were again ditches. In the eastern stretch there was a massive entrance, which has been reconstructed as a tower gateway projecting in front of the line of the rampart into the gap in the interrupted ditch.

The inner ditch varied in width according to the lie of the land. Behind the ditch rows of round post holes were then uncovered, replaced in some places by a continuous groove. In some places the holes survived in pairs and so formed two parallel rows. In front of the ditch of the southern and eastern stretches, at a distance of 4 to 5.8 m, there was a further ditch, whose depth was around 1.45 m and whose width at the top was about 3 m. In some places smaller round holes left by wooden posts were visible here too.

One approach to the hillfort was made possible by the narrow space created between the ditch and the barrier set out in front of it. It began at the point where the barrier was interrupted and continued southwards. The width of the passage was 4 to 5 m and it formed the gateway of the so-called side entrance. Crossing the ditch and entering the hillfort itself was probably made possible by a bridge over the ditch. The side gateway allowed those arriving to be checked, prevented a direct attack on the entrance to the hillfort and, if an enemy did penetrate into the narrow space, made it possible to attack and shoot at him from the flank. The strategic function of the side gateway was moreover strengthened by the lower position of the lane compared with the ground carrying the ditches and ramparts. The defenders standing on top of the rampart were at an advantageous higher point than the attacker, and the difference in height made it impossible for the besiegers to attack the rampart directly.

children.text: At the main entrance to the hillfort a wooden gateway with a tower superstructure was identified and reconstructed. The overall width of the gateway was about 7 m, and in its middle part the gateway was divided by a stout load-bearing post. The ceiling of the gateway was probably formed by a floor which took up the whole width of the entrance and gave access to the upper storey of the tower. The defenders on this floor were evidently protected by a wooden breastwork. The posts of the tower passed through this floor in its middle part. A raised storey in the tower with loopholes is also assumed. Because the gateway projected in front of the outer line of the rampart, the passage through it was 11 to 12 m long, and the width of both separate entrances was about 1.4 m. The entrance was therefore tight, but at the same time roomy enough for people, cattle and possibly narrower carts to pass through (as is also shown by the traces of a vehicle and the gauge of its wheels discovered at Klučov and at other sites). The entrances may have been closed by gates shutting off the whole space of the passage, but no traces of them were observed.
At one point in the defences the remains of a wooden tower were recognised, which also had an important role in the defence of the hillfort.

Exceptionally interesting was the discovery of an underground passage built at the north-western edge of the hillfort. The passage ran obliquely downwards as far as the level of the river and so gave the inhabitants of the hillfort access to a source of good water in the event of a siege.

The fortification of Klučov combined ancient structural elements reaching back to the Neolithic with the empirical experience of its builders, which could later be refined still further. The hillfort is among the oldest of its type, and the seemingly simple construction of the defences corresponds to this. The rampart did not, it is true, reach the height of the defences of later hillforts, but at a height of 2.5 m it presented, for the purposes of defence, an obstacle that could not easily be overcome with the ordinary means of the time. The height of the rampart was moreover strengthened by the ditch immediately in front of it.

The internal buildings were also investigated at the hillfort, where typical Slavic semi-sunken buildings and a larger number of granaries — pits intended for storing grain and food — were identified. It is precisely these features from Klučov that contributed significantly to our understanding of the internal buildings of Slavic hillforts and of the function of granaries in the early medieval period. Among the very interesting finds are also a well-preserved clay baking pan, several stone querns and many metal finds, which fill out the picture of life at the hillfort in the 8th and 9th centuries.
